label: CA firm capacity planning
overview: Capacity planning in a CA or advisory firm is the structured process of aligning available fee earner hours to the current and projected client workload — identifying surpluses and deficits before they become operational crises. The three capacity models (base capacity, scenario versioning, and client trimming) address different planning horizons and problems. Base capacity answers 'where are we now?' Scenario versioning answers 'what happens if we grow, shrink, or restructure?' Client trimming answers 'which clients are consuming capacity that should be redeployed?' All three must be run before any staffing or structural decision is made.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the capacity challenge a current-state measurement problem (the firm does not have clear visibility of available vs. committed hours), a future-state planning problem (a growth or restructuring decision requires modelling multiple scenarios), or a client portfolio optimisation problem (certain clients are consuming disproportionate capacity relative to their fee contribution)?
diagnostic_entry.current_state_measurement: Run the base capacity model first. Establish total available hours, actual utilisation by staff level, and WIP quantum by service line. This baseline is the prerequisite for any other capacity planning work — scenario modelling is meaningless without an accurate starting position.
diagnostic_entry.future_state_planning: Once the baseline is established, build the scenario version models. Scenarios should include at minimum: the status quo trajectory, a growth scenario (e.g. 20% WIP increase), and a structural change scenario (e.g. partner retirement, new service line, merger). Each scenario reveals different capacity requirements and informs staffing and investment decisions.
diagnostic_entry.client_portfolio_optimisation: If the base model reveals that overall capacity is adequate but certain fee earners are overloaded, run the client trimming analysis. Identify clients whose fee-to-hours ratio is below the firm's target return — these are candidates for fee renegotiation, service reduction, or managed exit. Releasing low-value client hours creates capacity for higher-value work without increasing headcount.

support_tools.name: Base Capacity Model
support_tools.purpose: Establishes the firm's current capacity position — the relationship between available fee earner hours, actual utilisation rates, and WIP demand — providing the factual baseline for all subsequent capacity planning decisions.
support_tools.core_principle: Most firms believe they know their capacity position but are operating on assumptions, not data. The base capacity model forces the conversion of assumptions into measured actuals — available hours minus non-billable time minus write-offs equals true productive capacity.
support_tools.when_to_use: Run at the start of any capacity engagement, at the beginning of each financial year, and whenever a material change (new hire, partner exit, service line change) occurs.

model_components.calculation: Standard working weeks per year × days per week × hours per day × number of fee earners
model_components.typical_adjustments: Deduct: annual leave (4-6 weeks), public holidays, CPD and training days, sick leave provision (3-5 days). Result is the gross available hours per annum.

model_components.description: The percentage of gross available hours that should be billable or client-chargeable. Industry benchmarks: senior partners 55-65%, managers 70-80%, senior staff 75-85%, junior staff 80-90%. Partners carry a higher non-billable load (business development, firm management, supervision) which explains the lower utilisation target.
model_components.calculation: Target Billable Hours = Gross Available Hours × Target Utilisation Rate

model_components.description: Measure actual billed and billable hours from the time recording system for the trailing 12 months. Compare to target utilisation. A persistent gap of more than 10 percentage points below target indicates a structural issue — poor work allocation, excessive non-billable time, or low WIP volume.
red_flags: Senior staff utilisation below 60% — likely a WIP shortage or poor allocation from partners
Junior staff utilisation above 90% — burnout risk; no buffer for quality review and CPD
High variance between fee earners in the same grade — unequal workload distribution

model_components.description: Map total WIP (contracted client work in progress) against the capacity required to deliver it. Segment by service line (compliance, tax, advisory, audit) and compare the WIP demand profile to the available capacity profile by skill level.
model_components.output: A clear picture of where capacity surplus or deficit exists by service line and skill level — the foundation for redeployment, recruitment, or client portfolio decisions.

support_tools.name: Scenario Versioning Model
support_tools.purpose: Projects the firm's capacity position under multiple defined future states — enabling the partnership to make staffing, investment, and structural decisions on the basis of modelled evidence rather than assumption.
support_tools.core_principle: A firm that only models its current position cannot make confident decisions about its future. Scenario versioning converts 'what if' questions into quantified capacity impacts, allowing the partnership to assess the staffing and financial implications of each strategic option before committing.
support_tools.when_to_use: Use when a material strategic decision is under consideration: growth targets, partner admission or retirement, merger or acquisition, new service line launch, or significant technology adoption. Each decision has a capacity implication that must be modelled before it is made.

standard_scenarios.description: Project current WIP growth rates forward using a 12-month rolling trend. Model the capacity requirement at 12 and 24 months if current growth continues without structural change. This scenario reveals whether the firm will hit a capacity ceiling on its current trajectory and when.
standard_scenarios.key_output: The month or quarter at which current staffing hits target utilisation ceiling — the trigger point for recruitment or service level reduction.

standard_scenarios.description: Model the capacity requirement if WIP grows by a defined percentage above the current trend (e.g. 20% or 30% growth scenarios from a marketing or BD initiative). Identify the staffing profile and cost required to service the growth.
standard_scenarios.key_output: The incremental headcount required at each staff level to service the growth scenario, with the associated payroll cost. Compare to the projected revenue from the additional WIP to assess whether the growth is financially viable.

standard_scenarios.description: Model the capacity impact of removing a partner from the billable pool, including both the direct loss of their billable hours and the client portfolio transition requirements. Quantify the expected client attrition risk and the capacity required by remaining staff to absorb the transitioned portfolio.
standard_scenarios.key_output: The net capacity impact (hours freed up from the departing partner's supervisory load versus client hours that must be absorbed), and the timeline over which the transition must be managed.

standard_scenarios.description: Model the capacity diversion required to build and deliver a new service line — including the learning curve period where fee earners are investing non-billable hours in capability development. Identify whether the new service line can be staffed from existing capacity or requires dedicated headcount.
standard_scenarios.key_output: The break-even point at which the new service line generates sufficient revenue to justify the capacity investment, and the minimum viable WIP required at launch to make the service line economically rational.

support_tools.name: Client Trimming Analysis
support_tools.purpose: Identifies clients whose fee-to-hours ratio is below the firm's target return, enabling a structured and commercially rational approach to either renegotiating those client relationships, reducing the service delivered, or managing an exit — releasing capacity for higher-value work.
support_tools.core_principle: Every hour invested in a below-target client is an hour not invested in a higher-value client or business development. Client trimming is not about abandoning clients — it is about ensuring the firm's most finite resource (experienced fee earner time) is deployed against the highest-value opportunities.
support_tools.when_to_use: Use when the firm is at or near capacity but revenue growth is lagging, when senior fee earners are consistently overloaded but billing targets are not being met, or when the firm is preparing to take on significant new WIP and needs to identify capacity without increasing headcount.

analysis_process.name: Fee Realisation Analysis
analysis_process.action: For each client, calculate the fee realisation rate: actual fees billed ÷ (hours worked × standard hourly rate). A realisation rate below 85% on a consistent basis indicates the client is being subsidised — either through write-offs, discounting, or scope creep absorption.
analysis_process.benchmark: Target realisation rate: 90-100%. Clients below 80% for more than two consecutive years are primary trimming candidates.

analysis_process.name: Strategic Value Assessment
analysis_process.action: Apply a qualitative filter to the below-target clients. Some may be below target because of a temporary situation (business going through a difficult period, relationship investment in a growing client) — these are not trimming candidates. Others may be chronically unprofitable with no strategic rationale — these are the primary targets.
strategic_value_factors: Growth trajectory of the client business
Profile or brand value in the firm's target market

analysis_process.name: Client Exit or Renegotiation Decision
analysis_process.action: For each identified trimming candidate, determine whether the relationship should be (a) renegotiated to a higher fee structure, (b) reduced to a lower service level the client accepts, or (c) managed to an exit. The decision depends on the client's likely response to each option and the firm's relationship capital with that client.
analysis_process.exit_management: A managed client exit requires a minimum 90-day notice period, a professional introduction to an alternative service provider, and a transition of all client files and records. A poorly managed exit creates reputational risk. A well-managed exit creates goodwill — the client may return as a better-fit client in the future.

analysis_process.name: Capacity Redeployment
analysis_process.action: Quantify the hours released by the trimming decisions and map them explicitly to the highest-value capacity applications identified in the base model — whether existing WIP that is under-resourced, new client acquisition, or service line development.
analysis_process.output: A documented capacity redeployment plan that connects the trimming decisions to specific, measurable outcomes — closing the loop between the analytical work and the commercial benefit.

support_tools.name: Capacity Planning — 5-Step Implementation Process
support_tools.purpose: Provides the sequenced implementation pathway for embedding capacity planning as an ongoing management practice in the firm — not as a one-off analytical exercise but as a quarterly discipline.
support_tools.core_principle: Capacity planning has no lasting value if it is performed once and shelved. The goal of the implementation process is to install the planning discipline into the firm's quarterly management rhythm — so that capacity decisions are made proactively, based on current data, rather than reactively, based on operational pain.
support_tools.when_to_use: Use after the initial base model and scenario analysis have been completed, to transition from a one-off engagement to an embedded management practice.

steps.name: Install Time Recording Discipline
steps.action: Capacity planning is only as accurate as the time recording data it is built on. Audit current time recording compliance — the percentage of fee earners recording time daily against client matters. Implement a mandatory daily time recording standard with a named partner accountable for compliance. A weekly compliance report should be reviewed at partner level.
steps.target: 95%+ daily time recording compliance across all fee earners within 60 days of the standard being set.

steps.name: Build the Capacity Dashboard
steps.action: Create a single-page capacity dashboard that shows, at a glance: total available hours, actual utilisation by staff level, WIP quantum by service line, and write-off rates by client and partner. The dashboard should be updated monthly from time recording data and reviewed at the monthly partner meeting.
steps.format: The dashboard does not need to be complex — a well-structured spreadsheet updated from the practice management system is sufficient. The discipline of reviewing it regularly matters more than the sophistication of the tool.

steps.name: Establish Quarterly Scenario Review
steps.action: At the start of each quarter, run a scenario review using the updated base model data. Update the growth and structural scenarios for changes in the WIP pipeline, staff changes, and strategic direction. Use the scenario outputs to make staffing and resourcing decisions for the coming quarter before the capacity constraint is felt.
steps.output: A quarterly capacity decision record — a documented record of what the model showed, what decisions were made, and the rationale. This creates an audit trail of capacity management decisions and provides the evidence base for future pattern recognition.

steps.name: Annual Client Portfolio Review
steps.action: Conduct the client trimming analysis annually as part of the firm's strategic planning cycle. Review fee realisation rates for all clients, apply the strategic value filter, and make formal decisions on client retention, renegotiation, or exit. Document the decisions and track the capacity released against the redeployment plan.
steps.timing: Align with the financial year end so that the capacity decisions inform the next year's budget and resourcing plan.

steps.name: Connect Capacity to Recruitment and Investment Decisions
steps.action: Establish a formal governance rule: no new hire is approved without a current capacity model showing that existing capacity cannot service the growth at target utilisation. This rule does not prevent recruitment — it ensures that recruitment decisions are based on evidence rather than instinct, and that the firm does not over-hire in a growth period and then face a capacity surplus when growth normalises.
steps.cultural_change: This step often requires a change in partner culture — shifting from 'we feel stretched, let's hire' to 'let's measure the constraint before we hire'. The data from steps 1-4 makes this cultural shift possible because it provides the evidence that replaces instinct.

support_tools.name: Capacity Planning — If-Then Guidance
support_tools.purpose: Decision logic for the most common capacity planning complications — utilisation variance, WIP growth outpacing headcount, senior staff bottlenecks, and scenario divergence from actuals.

if_then_logic.condition: Base model shows adequate average utilisation but specific staff are consistently overloaded
if_then_logic.action: Do not respond by hiring at the overloaded staff's level. Map the overloaded individual's WIP load by client and service line. Identify whether the overload is caused by insufficient delegation (work that could be handled by a junior staff member is being retained by the senior), or by a genuine specialisation bottleneck. Address delegation first — hiring before the delegation problem is solved will replicate the problem at the new hire level.

if_then_logic.condition: Scenario model shows the firm will hit a capacity ceiling within 6 months on the growth trajectory
if_then_logic.action: Begin the recruitment process immediately — the average recruitment, onboarding, and productive contribution timeline for a qualified CA hire is 3-6 months. Waiting until the capacity ceiling is reached means the firm will be operating above sustainable utilisation for the entire recruitment period, increasing write-off rates and burnout risk.

if_then_logic.condition: Client trimming analysis identifies a significant volume of below-target clients but exits would create a revenue gap
if_then_logic.action: Sequence the exits over 12-18 months, aligned to the business development pipeline's ability to replace the revenue. Calculate the net margin impact of each exit — a client at 70% realisation generating $50k revenue has a lower net margin contribution than the headline figure suggests. Replacing them with a 95% realisation client at $40k is a net positive margin outcome despite the lower revenue.

if_then_logic.condition: Capacity model actuals are consistently diverging from scenario projections
if_then_logic.action: Audit the quality of the time recording data. The most common source of scenario divergence is time recording that is being recorded against incorrect client or service line codes, creating a distorted picture of where capacity is being consumed. A data quality audit of time recording entries is required before the model can be trusted.

advisor_guidance.data_quality_determines_model_quality: Capacity planning is only as reliable as the time recording data it is built on. A firm that does not have consistent, accurate daily time recording cannot build a meaningful capacity model — the first intervention must be time recording compliance, not the analytical framework. Do not build the model on unreliable data and present it as fact.
advisor_guidance.scenario_modelling_changes_partner_behav: The most significant value of scenario modelling in a CA firm is not the output — it is the change in how the partnership discusses capacity. Partners who have seen the modelled impact of a partner retirement or a 25% growth scenario make fundamentally different resourcing decisions than partners who are operating on instinct. The model creates a shared evidence base that depersonalises what would otherwise be subjective debates.
advisor_guidance.client_trimming_requires_courage: Most CA firms know intuitively which clients are unprofitable but avoid acting on it because the relationship history, the discomfort of the exit conversation, and the short-term revenue impact feel more concrete than the long-term capacity benefit. The client trimming analysis converts the intuition into data, and the data makes the action possible. The advisor's role is to hold the data in front of the partnership until the decision is made.
advisor_guidance.capacity_planning_is_a_discipline_not_a_: The firms that benefit most from capacity planning are those that embed it as a quarterly discipline — not those that commission a one-off capacity review and shelve the model. The implementation process is designed to install the discipline, not just deliver an analysis. Measure the embedding success by whether the capacity dashboard is being reviewed monthly 12 months after the engagement.
